slides.title: In 1906, New Yorkers could stream music.
slides.sub: No one alive has heard it.

slides.kicker: A lawyer with a musical idea.
slides.body:
Thaddeus Cahill had studied the physics of music before training as a lawyer.

In 1897, he patented a bold plan: make music with electricity, and send it down telephone lines to anyone who wanted it.
Each rotor produced one pitch. Musicians at the keyboards mixed them, and the sound travelled over the phone network.

Cahill built his big machine in Holyoke, Massachusetts. In 1906, moving it to New York took around 30 railway boxcars.

It filled a whole floor below a music room at Broadway and 39th Street.

slides.kicker: Music on tap. 20 cents an hour.
slides.body:
Restaurants and hotels plugged in first. The music came out of telephone receivers fitted with horns.

Mark Twain was a fan.

The machine needed huge electric currents. Its music leaked into nearby phone lines and cut into ordinary calls.

In 1907, AT&T's head of engineering judged it would disturb regular phone service.

Partners left and the money ran out. Cahill filed for bankruptcy in 1914, and his machines were sold for scrap.

No recording survives. But its spinning-wheel idea lived on in the Hammond organ.

slides.lead: Being right about the future isn't enough.
slides.accent: The world also has to be ready for it.

slides.line: Save this for the next time you're early to an idea.

caption:
In 1906, inventor Thaddeus Cahill streamed electric music to New York restaurants and hotels over telephone lines, from a 200-ton machine called the Telharmonium. It was one of the first electronic instruments, and no recording of it survives.

Which invention do you think arrived too early?
